subject: botany
question_text: Write briefly about the different types of ovules.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack botany section (book pp.18-19, SAQ 5). Botany holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no botany board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The 1+1+1+1 split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The book covers only these three ovule types (no hemianatropous/amphitropous/circinotropous), and this card follows the book's scope. FIGURE SCOPE: the book prints three separate stippled drawings; this card draws the three side by side as simplified exam outlines with micropyle, chalaza, funicle and raphe labelled.

page_header: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants · 4 marks

steps.label: Basis of classification
lines: Ovules are classified by the position of the
micropyle with respect to the funicle and
steps.why: One sentence of basis makes the three definitions read as one system instead of three unrelated names — the micropyle's position is the thing that changes.
common_mistakes: Classifying by ovule size or by the number of integuments — the basis is the micropyle-funicle position.
steps.memory_tip: Watch the micropyle: straight up, folded down beside the stalk, or swung to the side.
steps.margin_note: Unmarked opening line — one sentence, then the three types.

steps.label: Orthotropous ovule
lines: chalaza and funicle lie in one straight
steps.why: This is the reference posture: the ovule stands upright on its stalk, so the three landmarks stack in a line — every other type is described as a change from this.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the example. Polygonum is the standard one.
Writing 'micropyle faces the funicle' — that is anatropous, the opposite of straight.
steps.memory_tip: ORTHO = straight (as in orthopaedics) — all three parts in one line.
steps.margin_note: Definition + example: two lines are enough for this mark.

steps.label: Anatropous ovule
lines: Anatropous (inverted) ovule: the body of the
ovule turns through 180°, so the micropyle
lies close to the funicle. A raphe is present.
steps.why: The full inversion is the identifying fact: after a 180° turn the micropyle ends up beside the stalk, and the fused part of the funicle along the body forms the ridge called the raphe.
common_mistakes: Drawing or describing the micropyle at the top — in an inverted ovule it points down beside the funicle.
Leaving out the raphe — it exists only because of the inversion, so examiners look for it.
steps.memory_tip: ANA-tropous = turned back: 180°, micropyle next to the funicle, raphe as the seam of the fold.
steps.margin_note: Say 180°, micropyle-near-funicle, and raphe — three facts, one mark.

steps.label: Campylotropous ovule
lines: Campylotropous ovule: the body of the ovule
is bent at a right angle to the funicle, and
the embryo sac is slightly curved.
steps.why: Between straight and fully inverted sits the bent form: the body turns only about 90°, so the ovule and its embryo sac both curve — the legumes are the standard examples.
common_mistakes: Writing 180° here — the right-angle bend is what separates it from anatropous.
Saying the embryo sac stays straight — in this type even the sac is slightly curved.
steps.memory_tip: CAMPYLO = bent (a camp-cot folds at an angle): body at 90°, sac slightly curved, pea and bean.
steps.margin_note: Right angle + curved sac + legume examples completes the trio.

steps.label: Diagram — the three ovule types
steps.why: The three postures are the answer — a straight stack, a full fold with the micropyle beside the funicle, and a right-angle bend. Drawing them side by side with the same three labels makes the comparison visible.
common_mistakes: Drawing anatropous with the micropyle at the top — the inversion is the whole point.
Labelling chalaza and micropyle at the same end. They are always opposite ends of the ovule body.
steps.memory_tip: Draw the funicle first in each, then place the micropyle: in line, beside it, at an angle.
steps.margin_note: Three small sketches with micropyle, chalaza and funicle labelled — 3-4 minutes.

insider_note: The diagram is where this question is really scored: the anatropous drawing with the micropyle beside the funicle is the detail that separates a 4 from a 3.
